The room had no windows and too much yellow light. It made everybody look guilty.

Detective Rourke sat across from me, his tie loose, his face polished with sweat. His partner, Bell, stood by the filing cabinet, smoking a cigarette down to the paper. Cheap tobacco. It hung in the air like a wet coat.

“You saw the girl leave the hotel,” Rourke said.

“I saw a lot of people leave a lot of places.”

He nodded to Bell.

Bell picked up the phone book from the table. Thick city directory, soft corners, names of the living and the dead all packed inside. He folded it in half and brought it down against my ribs.

The sound was a dull thump. The pain was not.

I sucked air through my teeth and kept my face still. A bruise tells a story. A phone book leaves the body to do its own talking.

“Try again,” Rourke said.

I tasted copper where I’d bitten my cheek. The tobacco smell crawled into my nose, bitter and cheap. I thought of the rain outside, washing the street clean for nobody.

“I told you,” I said. “I saw a lot of people.”

Bell hit me again. The directory swallowed the sound. My ribs didn’t.

Rourke leaned forward, elbows on the table. “You’re making this harder than it needs to be.”

“That’s funny,” I said. “I was thinking the same thing about your police work.”

Bell smiled without warmth and shifted the book in his hands.

Somewhere down the hall, a typewriter clacked on. The city kept making records. I wondered how much of me would be left by the time they finished mine.

The bag sat between them on the saloon table, its drawstring dark with sweat. Every so often a coin shifted inside with a small, bright clink.

“You said we’d split it,” Harlan said.

“I said we’d talk about splitting it.” Boone kept one hand beside the bag. His other rested near his belt. Around them, the saloon had gone quiet. A chair creaked. Somewhere behind the bar, a glass touched wood and stopped.

Harlan’s eyes stayed on Boone’s hand. “That’s a mighty narrow kind of talk.”

Boone smiled without warmth. “You always were bad at listening.”

Harlan reached for the bag.

Boone’s knife came out with a scrape of leather. The blade caught the lamplight. Harlan jerked back, knocking his chair over, and the room seemed to draw one breath.

“Put it down,” Harlan said.

“Take the money and find out.”

Harlan lunged. He caught Boone’s wrist with both hands, and they slammed into the table. The bag toppled, spilling gold across the floor in a hard, glittering scatter. Boone drove his shoulder into Harlan’s chest. Harlan stumbled into the bar, knocking bottles loose. One shattered. The stink of whiskey rose sharp over the dust and sweat.

They grappled in the narrow space, boots skidding on spilled liquor. Boone’s knife hand was trapped between them. Harlan twisted, trying to force it down; Boone shoved back, teeth bared. Then Harlan slipped.

Harlan made a short, shocked sound and clamped his other hand over the cut. Blood welled between his fingers, darkening his sleeve. He dropped to one knee, more from surprise than pain, then sucked in a breath that shook on the way out.

Boone stood over him, chest heaving, the knife still raised. For a moment neither man moved. Coins lay scattered around Harlan’s boots.

“Now,” Harlan said, voice thin but steady, “you’ve got your half.”

The bartender had a shotgun leveled across the counter. “Nobody’s got anything,” he said. “Not till I say so.”

Boone looked at the gun, then at the blood running down Harlan’s wrist. Slowly, he lowered the knife.

Marek set the rifle components in order and covered them with the towel.

The basement door opened an inch, then stopped against something soft.

Mara pushed harder.

The door dragged over the concrete with a low, reluctant scrape. A smell climbed the stairs to meet her: damp earth, hot metal, and the sweet-sour staleness of a room sealed too long. She covered her mouth with her sleeve. It did nothing.

The single bulb overhead swung in a slow circle, making the basement appear and disappear in pieces.

Cal was slumped beside the furnace, his knees drawn up as if he’d sat down to rest. One sneaker had come off. His glasses lay several feet away, one lens catching the light, then losing it. Mara took one step toward him and heard the wet tack of her shoe peeling off the floor.

She looked down.

A dark smear crossed the concrete beneath her feet. It vanished under a workbench, where the shadows were thickest.

“No,” she whispered.

The bulb swung back.

Nina lay near the bottom of the stairs, one arm stretched toward the light switch. Her bright yellow sweater was dulled with dust, her hair spread across the floor like spilled ink. She looked almost asleep. That was the worst part: the stillness, the suggestion that if Mara said her name loudly enough, Nina might stir and complain about the cold.

At the far wall, Owen sat upright in an old wooden chair. His head had fallen forward. The chair gave a faint creak as the bulb’s pull-chain tapped it, again and again—tiny, patient knocks.

Mara backed into the railing. It rattled under her hand.

The basement had its own weather. Cold pooled around her ankles; the air tasted of rust and mildew. Somewhere behind the furnace, water dripped at steady intervals. Each drop sounded like a footstep starting and stopping.

Then the bulb swung away, and the room went black.

In the darkness, something shifted.

Mara held her breath. The silence pressed close, full of the small sounds she hadn’t noticed before: the hum of the furnace, the tick of cooling pipes, the tremble of her own pulse in her ears.

The light returned.

Owen was still in the chair. Cal was still by the furnace. Nina still reached for the switch.

But behind the workbench, where the shadows had been thickest, a pale hand now rested on the concrete.

Mara ran for the stairs. Behind her, the basement door began to swing shut.

The prison was built beneath a mountain, where no signal could reach it and no sunrise could be seen.

They called it the Continuance. The officials said it was humane. No cells with bars, no years spent staring at concrete. Instead, each inmate was fitted with a silver crown and made to live, for a few minutes at a time, inside the memories of the people they had harmed.

“Not punishment,” the warden liked to say. “Understanding.”

Marek had heard that phrase so often it had become another wall.

On his first morning in the Continuance, the crown settled around his skull. The technician asked if he was ready.

“No,” Marek said.

The technician looked to the warden.

“Begin,” said the warden.

The room vanished.

Marek was standing in a kitchen he had never seen. A yellow cup sat beside the sink. A child’s drawing was held to the refrigerator by a magnet shaped like a pear. Rain tapped at the window.

For one suspended second, he was only looking.

Then he understood that he wasn’t looking through someone else’s eyes. He was looking with them.

A woman’s hands were gripping the edge of the counter. Her name, he somehow knew, was Lena. Her heart was beating too fast. She had a headache behind her left eye. She was thinking she ought to buy milk on the way home tomorrow.

Then she heard the knock.

Marek felt her stop breathing.

The terror did not arrive as a scream. It arrived as arithmetic. The distance to the back door. The weight of the phone in her pocket. The child asleep upstairs. The fact that the hallway was too long and the door too close to the person outside.

Her mind reached for ordinary explanations and found none.

Marek tried to move. He tried to shut his eyes. But the memory had no darkness he could choose. He was locked inside the woman’s attention as it narrowed, each detail brightening with unbearable importance: the wet footprints on the mat, the knife block by the sink, the tiny tremor in her thumb.

The door opened.

He felt Lena recognize him.

Not his face, not yet. His voice. The one he had used when he told her he only wanted to talk. The one she had believed, for half a minute, because she had wanted to believe it.

The memory lurched forward. A chair scraped. A glass fell and shattered. Lena’s body was moving before her thoughts could catch up, one hand raised, not to fight but to protect her head.

Marek had remembered that night as anger. A blur. A mistake that had taken less than a minute.

Inside Lena, time thickened.

There was the shock of the first impact—not pain, exactly, but the sudden impossibility of what was happening. Then fear, vast and practical. She was afraid of dying. She was afraid of leaving her child alone upstairs. She was afraid that the child would wake and come looking for her.

Most of all, she was afraid because she could hear the child stir.

Marek felt her try to call out. Her throat would not obey.

He felt her bargain with the world: Let him stop. Let the child stay asleep. Let there be a tomorrow with milk in the refrigerator and the yellow cup by the sink.

There was no tomorrow in the memory. There was only the shrinking room, the rain, the pear magnet, the upstairs floorboard creaking beneath a small foot.

Then the fear broke open—not into peace, but into one final, desperate thought:

Please don’t let him see.

The world went black.

Marek woke on the floor of the immersion room, retching. A nurse held his shoulders. The crown was already gone.

The warden stood beyond her, hands folded behind his back.

“Do you understand now?” he asked.

Marek couldn’t answer. Lena’s fear still filled the spaces between his ribs. It had no lesson in it, no clean instruction, no door leading out. It was simply what she had lived through, and what he had made happen.

For days he could not bear the sound of rain.

The Continuance ran the memory again the following week. And the week after that. They said repetition would help him process it. Perhaps they were right. He learned every detail: the yellow cup, the pear magnet, the child’s foot on the stair.

He never learned how to make the memory smaller.

Years later, when a new inmate asked him what the crown did, Marek told him the truth.

“It doesn’t put you in their shoes,” he said. “It shows you that they were never shoes. They were a whole life. And you don’t get to step out of it just because you’re done feeling sorry.”

Marek was standing in a kitchen he had never seen. A yellow cup sat beside the sink. A child’s drawing was held to the refrigerator by a magnet shaped like a pear. Rain tapped at the window.

For one suspended second, he was only looking.

Then he understood that he wasn’t looking through someone else’s eyes. He was looking with them.

A woman’s hands were gripping the edge of the counter. Her name, he somehow knew, was Lena. Her heart was beating too fast. She had a headache behind her left eye. She was thinking she ought to buy milk on the way home tomorrow.

Then she heard the knock.

Marek felt her stop breathing.

The terror did not arrive as a scream. It arrived as arithmetic. The distance to the back door. The weight of the phone in her pocket. The child asleep upstairs. The fact that the hallway was too long and the door too close to the person outside.

Her mind reached for ordinary explanations and found none.

Marek tried to move. He tried to shut his eyes. But the memory had no darkness he could choose. He was locked inside the woman’s attention as it narrowed, each detail brightening with unbearable importance: the wet footprints on the mat, the knife block by the sink, the tiny tremor in her thumb.

The door opened.

He felt Lena recognize him.

Not his face, not yet. His voice. The one he had used when he told her he only wanted to talk. The one she had believed, for half a minute, because she had wanted to believe it.

The memory lurched forward. A chair scraped. A glass fell and shattered. Lena’s body was moving before her thoughts could catch up, one hand raised, not to fight but to protect her head.

Marek had remembered that night as anger. A blur. A mistake that had taken less than a minute.

Inside Lena, time thickened.

There was the shock of the first impact—not pain, exactly, but the sudden impossibility of what was happening. Then fear, vast and practical. She was afraid of dying. She was afraid of leaving her child alone upstairs. She was afraid that the child would wake and come looking for her.

Most of all, she was afraid because she could hear the child stir.

Marek felt her try to call out. Her throat would not obey.

He felt her bargain with the world: Let him stop. Let the child stay asleep. Let there be a tomorrow with milk in the refrigerator and the yellow cup by the sink.

There was no tomorrow in the memory. There was only the shrinking room, the rain, the pear magnet, the upstairs floorboard creaking beneath a small foot.

Then the fear broke open—not into peace, but into one final, desperate thought:

Please don’t let him see.

The world went black.

Marek woke on the floor of the immersion room, retching. A nurse held his shoulders. The crown was already gone.

The warden stood beyond her, hands folded behind his back.

“Do you understand now?” he asked.

Marek couldn’t answer. Lena’s fear still filled the spaces between his ribs. It had no lesson in it, no clean instruction, no door leading out. It was simply what she had lived through, and what he had made happen.

For days he could not bear the sound of rain.

The Continuance ran the memory again the following week. And the week after that. They said repetition would help him process it. Perhaps they were right. He learned every detail: the yellow cup, the pear magnet, the child’s foot on the stair.

He never learned how to make the memory smaller.

Years later, when a new inmate asked him what the crown did, Marek told him the truth.

“It doesn’t put you in their shoes,” he said. “It shows you that they were never shoes. They were a whole life. And you don’t get to step out of it just because you’re done feeling sorry.”

Mara heard the footsteps stop when she stopped.

The woods held their breath around her. She stood beneath a leaning pine, one hand pressed to the stitch in her side, and listened to the dark behind her. Nothing. Then, from somewhere beyond the trees, came a soft, wet crack.

She ran.

Branches whipped her face. The path dipped toward the creek, moonlight flashing between trunks. Behind her, something crashed through the undergrowth—not running like a man, not quite. Too heavy. Too fast.

Mara glanced back.

A shape stood in the clearing.

At first she thought it was a person bent double, hands braced on its knees. Then its shoulders jerked upward with a sound like green wood splitting. It cried out, and the cry broke halfway through: a man’s voice swallowed by a growl.

Mara stumbled against a tree.

The creature’s back arched. Its spine rose beneath its coat, each vertebra pressing into the fabric as if something inside were trying to climb out. Another crack snapped through the clearing. It dropped to one knee, fingers clawing the dirt. The hands shuddered, knuckles swelling, nails darkening and curving into points.

She should have run. She couldn’t make her legs obey.

The coat strained across its shoulders. Seams popped one after another. Beneath them, skin pulled tight, shining pale in the moonlight. The creature bucked and groaned as its arms lengthened, elbows shifting with a series of ugly clicks. Its jaw thrust forward. The skin along its face stretched taut, then split at the corners of its mouth—not a gush of blood, just a thin, dark line, like a smile being forced too wide.

Mara covered her own mouth to keep from making a sound.

The thing lifted its head. Its eyes found hers, still human for one terrible second. In them she saw recognition. Shame. A plea.

Then the pupils widened until the eyes were black.

Fur rippled over its shoulders and down its arms. Its teeth crowded forward, catching the moonlight. When it stood, it had to unfold itself in stages, joints cracking as it rose taller than any man. The ruined coat hung from it in strips.

Mara backed away.

One paw touched the ground.

The creature’s nostrils flared. It smelled her fear—or the blood on her scraped palm—and lowered its head.

Then it began to follow.

results.model_response:
The fever came on with the rain.

By midnight, Mara was shivering beneath two coats in the ticket office, though the stove glowed red and the rest of them had stripped down to shirtsleeves. She kept apologizing for the damp footprints she’d left on the floor.

“It’s all right,” Jonah said, for the sixth time.

“I know.” Her teeth clicked together. “I just keep thinking about the floor.”

No one laughed. They had all laughed at worse things, once. Before the sirens stopped. Before a bite became a clock.

The bandage around Mara’s forearm had gone dark. She’d taken the teeth there while pulling Tomas from beneath a bus. They’d washed it. Bound it. Prayed, though no one used that word. Now a thin black line crept up from the bandage, disappearing beneath her sleeve.

At the window, Inez watched the rain crawl down the glass. “We said we’d decide at first sign.”

“This is a fever,” Jonah said.

“It’s the line.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I do.”

“Then why are you looking out the window?”

Inez turned. Her face was exhausted, not angry. “Because I don’t want to look at her.”

Mara opened her eyes. “That’s fair.”

Jonah sank to his knees beside her. “Don’t.”

“I’m not accusing her.” Mara swallowed. “Or you.”

He took her uninjured hand. It was hot and dry against his palm. A year ago, she’d held that same hand while he shook with hunger, telling him the canned peaches were real and not a dream. Now he couldn’t stop staring at the small scars across her knuckles.

“We can wait,” he said.

“For what?”

“For morning.”

“And if I’m not me in the morning?”

“You will be.”

She studied him with the patience she’d used on frightened children. “You don’t know that.”

“I know you.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

Behind them, Tomas made a sound in his throat. He sat against the wall, wrapped in a blanket, face hidden. He had been the reason Mara was bitten. He had not spoken since.

Inez came to stand by the door. “If she turns in here—”

“Don’t,” Jonah said.

“I have to say it.”

“No. You don’t.”

Mara squeezed his hand. The pressure was weak, but deliberate. “Jonah. Look at me.”

He did.

“I don’t want to wake up hungry.”

The room seemed to contract around the words. Rain tapped the broken panes. Somewhere far off, something called through the dark and was answered.

Jonah shook his head. “You’re asking me to—”

“I’m asking you to stay with me.”

“That isn’t the same.”

“No,” she whispered. “It isn’t.”

Her breathing hitched. She closed her eyes until it passed. When she opened them again, she looked frightened, and that was worse than the fever. Jonah had seen Mara frightened only once before: when she thought the baby they’d found in the pharmacy had stopped breathing. She had been frightened then, too, and had kept working.

Inez placed the revolver on the floor between them, not offering it to anyone. Just setting down the fact of it.

Jonah stared at the gun. The decision seemed too small to contain what it meant. One hand’s reach. One motion. A before and an after, with nothing between.

Tomas lifted his face from the blanket. “It should be me.”

Mara turned her head. “You’re not bitten.”

“I got you—”

“You got me out.”

“I could’ve—”

“Don’t make this about what you owe.”

Tomas began to cry. Quietly, as though he were ashamed to be heard.

Mara shifted her fingers around Jonah’s. “Tell me something ordinary.”

He couldn’t think of anything. The world had taken ordinary things and made them relics.

“Tell me what you’re going to do tomorrow,” she said.

He forced himself to breathe. “Fix the north window.”

“You hate fixing windows.”

“I hate fixing that window.”

A faint smile touched her mouth. “And after?”

“Find coffee.”

“You always say that.”

“One day I’ll find it.”

“There you go.”

Her skin was burning now. Jonah felt it through their joined hands. He bent until his forehead rested against hers. For a moment, there was only the rain and her breath, warm against his cheek.

When he pulled away, Mara was watching him.

“I’m here,” he said.

“I know.”

He picked up the revolver. His hand shook so badly that Inez stepped forward, then stopped when Mara shook her head.

Jonah held Mara’s gaze. He wanted to ask permission again, though she had given it. He wanted her to take it back. He wanted the fever to be a fever, the line to be ink, the world to open its doors and let them all go home.

Instead, Mara touched his wrist.

“Stay,” she said.

He stayed.

The sound was brief. The silence afterward was not.

For a long time, no one moved. Jonah kept hold of her hand until the heat began to leave it. Then he set the revolver on the floor and bowed over her, his shoulders shaking without a sound.

Outside, the rain kept falling.

In the morning, the north window still needed fixing.

results.model_response:
At first, the ghost appeared only in the corner of his eye: a pale shape where the hallway darkened, a shoulder slipping behind a doorway. Each time he turned, there was nothing there.

He learned to live with the almost-seeing. He stopped looking directly at empty corners. He kept lamps burning, though the light made the rooms feel exposed rather than safe. At night he listened for the small sounds of the house—the pipes ticking, the floor settling—and found in each one the beginning of a footstep.

The rot was gradual. It worked on the ordinary parts of him first. He forgot what he had gone into a room to do. He read the same sentence until the words lost their meaning. When someone spoke his name, he flinched, certain they had discovered something in his face.

Then the ghost began appearing in reflections. A smear of pallor behind him in the dark window. A familiar tilt of the head in the mirror, gone when he looked over his shoulder. He told himself it was exhaustion, then shadows, then the mind searching for what it feared. The explanations comforted him less each time.

He started rehearsing conversations with the dead: apologies, excuses, bargains. In his imagination, the victim never raised their voice. They only watched him with the patient attention of someone waiting for him to finish lying.

Soon he could no longer tell whether he feared being caught or feared the moment the watching would stop. He had wanted the murder to close a door. Instead, it had left him living in a house full of thresholds, forever sensing someone just beyond them.

The room had no windows. It had a drain in the floor and a clock whose second hand clicked loudly enough to count the silence.

“Where is the radio?”

He tried to answer. His mouth was dry; his tongue felt too large. He said nothing.

Then the world narrowed to cloth, weight, and water.

His body knew what was happening before his mind could name it. He bucked against the restraints. Air vanished—not slowly, not like sinking beneath a lake, but all at once, as if the room had decided he no longer belonged to the breathing world.

His chest convulsed. His throat clenched. Somewhere inside him, a frantic animal beat against the walls of his ribs.

There was no sea, no depth, no darkness to swim toward. He was still in the room. He could hear the clock. He could hear someone speaking. His heels scraped the surface beneath him, absurdly close to solid ground.

That was the worst of it: the knowledge that he was not drowning, and the certainty that he was.

A hand lifted. The water stopped.

He dragged in a breath that tore through him. It sounded ragged and unfamiliar. His eyes streamed; the room blurred into a light, a shoulder, the hard line of a table. He tried to cough and couldn’t make his body obey. Each breath came with a shudder, each pause filled by the memory of the next one being taken away.

“Where is the radio?” the voice asked again.

He stared at the clock. Its second hand kept moving.

For a moment, that small, indifferent motion was the only thing he could believe in. Then the question came again, and the room began to shrink.

The rain over New Carthage came down in silver threads, catching the glow of the transit towers.

Mara Venn found her target beneath the old maglev station, where the city’s lights thinned and the abandoned platforms hummed with buried power. Jace Orlan stood at the end of the platform, one hand wrapped around a stolen data core.

“Bounty’s for alive,” Mara called. “Let’s keep it that way.”

Jace bolted.

He vaulted a maintenance rail and charged her when she cut him off. Mara raised her stun weapon and fired. Its blue-white arc snapped across the gap.

The shock locked Jace’s muscles in a sudden, involuntary spasm. His arms jerked tight against his sides; his legs failed to support him, and he hit the platform hard. A sharp cry escaped him before he could catch his breath. For a few seconds he could only tremble, dazed and unable to coordinate his movements.

Mara was beside him as soon as the current stopped. She kicked the data core out of reach, then crouched without touching his neck or chest.

“Can you hear me?”

Jace blinked, gasping. “Yeah.”

“Good. Stay still.”

A stun charge could do more than hurt: powerful electrical currents could disrupt normal muscle control, interfere with breathing, and, in rare cases, disturb the heart’s rhythm. Mara had no way to know what his body had endured until she checked him. She called for a medical unit and watched his breathing while the station’s security drones sealed the exits.

When Jace tried to sit up, she gently pressed him back down.

“Don’t,” she said. “You’re captured. You’re also getting checked out.”

By the time the medics arrived, the rain had stopped. Mara stood over the stolen core, listening to the city wake above them, while Jace—shaken, angry, and alive—was eased onto a stretcher.

Mara woke to the sound of her own breathing, too loud in the dark.

A strip of white light cut across the room. Beyond it, a door stood open—close enough to see, impossibly far away. The speaker above her crackled, then delivered its message in a calm, almost courteous voice: the lock would release only when she paid its price.

She stared at the device beside her. The instructions were simple. That was the cruelty of them.

“No,” she whispered, though there was nobody to persuade.

Her first instinct was to bargain with the room. She tested the door, the walls, the straps holding her in place. She called for help until her throat rasped. Each failure narrowed the world to the choice waiting in front of her.

Mara thought of the people who would be searching for her. Then she thought of the voice on the speaker, and anger rose through the panic—hot, useful, almost steadying. Whoever had built this wanted her to believe there was only one thing she could do. They wanted her to mistake obedience for survival.

But the timer kept counting.

She shut her eyes and pressed her forehead to the cold floor. In. Out. The breaths came unevenly, but they came. She gathered her hair away from her face, planted her feet, and flexed her fingers until the trembling eased—not gone, just something she could carry. She looked toward the door again and fixed her attention on it: the pale rectangle of light, the open space beyond.

“I’m getting out,” she said.

Her hands moved into position. For one suspended moment, she remained perfectly still, caught between the person she had been before waking and the person the trap was trying to make of her.

Then she made herself act.

The lock snapped open. Mara staggered toward the light, one arm clutched against her chest, refusing to look back at the room.

The captain drew his saber and pointed it toward the narrow plank jutting over the sea.

“Your last step aboard the *Widow’s Wake*, Mr. Vale.”

Vale stared down. Moonlight silvered the waves, and beneath them dark shapes moved in slow circles. A fin broke the surface, vanished, then appeared again farther off. The sharks had caught the scent of the ship’s fear—or perhaps only the scraps tossed overboard at sunset.

Vale’s boots scraped against the deck as two sailors marched him forward. He tried to speak, but the words came out thin and breathless.

“You said the crew deserved a better captain,” the captain said. “Now you may find one below.”

The plank groaned under Vale’s weight. Wind tugged at his coat. Behind him, the crew stood silent; ahead, the sea heaved black and restless. He looked down again. A pale flash rolled beneath the surface, close enough to make his knees buckle.

“I’ll serve,” he pleaded. “I’ll do anything.”

The captain’s expression did not change. “You should have thought of that before you raised your knife.”

Vale edged forward. One step. Then another. The ship’s lanterns dwindled behind him, and the ocean filled his vision. A fin cut across the water beneath his shadow.

He froze at the plank’s end, shaking so hard the boards trembled with him. For one long moment, even the captain said nothing.

Then the wind shifted, and the *Widow’s Wake* creaked around him like a door slowly closing.

The first thing Mara felt was the pressure: a hard, unnatural band cinched across her ribs, holding her breath shallow. Then came the wires against her skin—thin, cool strands snagging at her shirt whenever she moved. She tried to lift a hand and stopped halfway, afraid even the smallest shift might make them twitch.

Tick.

The sound came from somewhere beneath the casing. Small. Patient.

Tick.

Her mouth went dry. She looked down, then away, then down again, as if the thing might disappear if she refused to see it. The wires blurred. Her heartbeat crowded out the room, but beneath it the ticking kept its steady pace.

“Help me,” she said. It came out almost calmly.

Then she heard the tremor in her own voice. Her hands began to shake. She clamped them against her sides, but the contact only made the wires prickle against her skin. A breath caught in her throat and broke into a laugh—one sharp, disbelieving sound.

Tick.

“No, no, no.” The words spilled faster now. “Don’t touch it. Don’t—please, just—”

The walls seemed to draw closer. She could feel every wire, every point of pressure, every second passing. Her thoughts scattered, each one louder than the last, until there was room for only the ticking and the ragged, rising pitch of her own panic.

Mara kept one hand on the wall and the other wrapped around her phone. The flashlight was on, but its beam trembled with every step, catching doorframes and furniture in brief, crooked slices.

The power had gone out without warning. One moment the kitchen clock was blinking; the next, the house had gone quiet except for the rain ticking against the windows.

“Eli?” she called.

Her brother was supposed to be upstairs. No answer.

The beam slid over the living-room sofa, the folded blanket, the open doorway to the hall. Everything looked ordinary, which somehow made it worse. Mara edged forward, toes feeling for the rug before she trusted her weight to it.

Behind her, in the shadow between the coat closet and the front door, a figure stood perfectly still.

Mara reached the hall. The phone’s light jumped over the staircase. At the top, a bedroom door stood ajar.

“Eli, stop messing around.”

A floorboard creaked upstairs.

She froze. The sound had come from above—or maybe from somewhere behind her. In the dark, the house seemed to have too many corners.

Mara turned slowly. The beam passed across the living room again. Sofa. Table. Curtains.

It stopped on the front door.

The door was still locked.

She let out a breath and continued toward the stairs. The light shook over the banister. Halfway there, she heard the softest scrape from the room behind her, like a shoe shifting on hardwood.

Mara swung around.

Nothing.

Her thumb slipped against the phone screen. The flashlight flickered off, then on. For one sharp instant, the light landed on a glint near the closet—a thin, bright line at waist height.

Then the beam jerked away.

She stood listening, her breath too loud in the narrow hall. The rain tapped the windows. Somewhere in the kitchen, the refrigerator gave a low click as it cooled in the dark.

“Who’s there?”

No answer.

Mara backed toward the stairs, keeping the phone aimed at the closet. The shadows there were solid, crowded together. She tried to remember the emergency number, the address, whether the back door was locked.

A faint sound came from just behind her.

Not a footstep. A breath.

She spun, and the flashlight swept across the room too fast to make sense of anything. By the time it steadied, the hall was empty.

But the front door, still locked a moment ago, now stood open by an inch.

The ration bell rang once.

Around the arena, thousands of people lifted their empty hands. The guards had promised bread to the winner and a week’s water to the district that cheered loudest. No one cheered.

Mara stood in the sand with a cracked shield strapped to her arm. Across from her, Tovin held a short spear in both hands. He was younger than she was, but not by much. They had shared a queue at the ration windows for years. Once, he had given her half an apple.

The announcer’s voice boomed from the towers. “Begin.”

Tovin came forward fast. Mara caught the spear on her shield, felt the impact shudder through her shoulder, and stumbled. The crowd stirred—not with excitement, but with the restless sound of people counting what they might eat.

He lunged again. She turned aside. His spear glanced off her ribs and tore her coat. Mara struck his wrist with the rim of her shield. The spear fell into the sand.

For a moment, neither moved.

Then Tovin looked up at the ration box above the arena gate. His little sister’s district mark was painted on its side.

Mara understood. So did he.

He charged barehanded. She could have stepped away. Instead she raised the shield, caught him against it, and drove the broken edge of her sword beneath his collarbone in one swift, desperate thrust.

Tovin went still. His fingers closed once around her sleeve, then slipped free. Mara lowered him carefully to the sand.

The bell rang again.

A gate opened. Behind it, a stack of ration tins gleamed beneath the white lights. The crowd remained silent as Mara walked toward them, carrying the weight of the week’s food in both hands.

Mara told herself she wasn’t trying to kill anyone.

She was only giving Victor the same fear he’d given her—one sharp, helpless moment in which the world stopped obeying him. He had ruined her brother’s life and called it business. He had smiled in court. Every ordinary remedy had failed, and Mara had begun to think that justice was just a word people used when they still had options.

So she tampered with his car and went home, repeating that he would notice in time. That he would be frightened, not hurt. That if something happened, it would be Victor’s fault for driving the way he always did.

At dawn, she watched from her kitchen window as he backed out. He turned the corner and disappeared.

Mara waited for the relief she’d imagined. Instead, the silence in the room grew enormous. She picked up the phone and called the police—not to confess, she told herself, but to warn them.

For the first time, the excuse sounded smaller than the thing she’d done.

The dog lunged before he could raise the scrap.

He hit the ground hard, the food crushed between his fist and his chest. Its growl rattled against his ribs. He drove a forearm under its jaw and shoved, boots scraping uselessly through ash and broken glass. The dog snapped at his sleeve, teeth catching cloth. He twisted away with a cry, then slammed his shoulder into it—not to hurt it so much as to make space enough to breathe.

The scrap slipped from his hand.

For one awful second they both saw it lying in the dirt.

He moved first. Hunger moved him. It had hollowed him out for days, turned every thought toward the ache beneath his ribs. He grabbed the food and curled over it as the dog snapped at his back. His elbow struck its shoulder; the dog yelped and recoiled. He scrambled upright, staggering, clutching the scrap in both hands.

The animal stood a few paces away, trembling with the same need.

He backed off, panting, unable to take his eyes from its teeth. The food shook in his grip. He knew he should run. Instead he tore off a piece and threw it hard into the dust. The dog darted after it.

He ran in the other direction, the rest of the food pressed to his mouth, eating as he stumbled—too fast to taste, too hungry to care.

The shot had taken Tomas high in the thigh. By the time Mara dragged him behind the overturned truck, his trouser leg was black with blood.

“Don’t look,” she said.

“I’m looking,” Tomas rasped. His face had gone the color of wet paper. “It’s my leg.”

Mara had a knife and a bottle of whiskey. Nothing else. No bandages, no proper tools, no one coming fast enough.

She poured the whiskey over the blade. It ran off in shining threads, carrying the smell of oak and smoke. Tomas watched her hand tremble.

“That won’t make it clean,” he said.

“No,” Mara answered. “It won’t.”

The wound was a torn, ugly thing, the cloth around it stuck to the skin. When she pulled the fabric aside, Tomas jerked so hard his head struck the truck’s metal frame. A raw cry burst out of him, then broke into ragged breaths.

Mara gripped his shoulder. “Stay with me.”

“I am with you.”

She worked as carefully as she could, but care didn’t make it gentle. Tomas screamed once—one sharp, disbelieving sound—and then bit down on his sleeve until the cloth darkened with spit and blood. His whole body shuddered beneath her hand. The knife slipped; she stopped, swearing under her breath, and pressed her palm against him until the worst of the bleeding slowed.

The whiskey bottle lay on its side in the dust. Its remaining contents glimmered amber in the firelight.

Tomas’s eyes found hers. “Did you get it?”

“I don’t know.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

For a moment, the only sounds were distant gunfire and Tomas trying to breathe through the pain. Mara leaned her forehead against his, both of them slick with sweat and blood.

“Keep talking,” she whispered.

“About what?”

“Anything.”

He swallowed, face twisting. “You still owe me a bottle.”

A laugh escaped her, small and frightened. “Then you’d better live long enough to collect.”

“Tell me the password,” Vale said.

Mara stared at the table. The lamp above it hummed softly, the only sound in the room.

“You’ve asked me that already.”

“And you’ve answered with silence.” Vale pulled a chair closer, its legs scraping the floor. “Silence is a choice. So is what happens next.”

Mara looked up. “You’re trying to make me imagine it.”

“I don’t have to try. You’re doing that yourself.”

For a moment, neither spoke. Vale set a small metal instrument on the table—not using it, just letting it catch the light.

Mara’s jaw tightened.

“Your hands are shaking,” Vale said. “That’s your body making the decision before you do.”

“My hands are cold.”

“Then let’s not waste time warming them.” Vale leaned in. “The password.”

Mara swallowed. “I don’t know it.”

“You do. You’re just hoping I’ll believe you long enough for someone to come looking.” Vale tapped the instrument once against the tabletop. “No one is coming through that door.”

Mara’s eyes flicked toward it.

“There,” Vale murmured. “That’s the moment you stop waiting for rescue and start thinking clearly.”

“What if I give you the wrong one?”

“Then we’ll both know you’re still bargaining.”

The hum of the lamp seemed louder. Mara closed her eyes, then opened them again.

“Say it,” Vale said. His voice was almost gentle. “Make this the last question.”

Mara drew a slow breath. “You’re not getting it.”

Vale stood. The chair scraped backward.

“Perhaps not,” he said. “But you’re going to hear that door stay closed for a while yet.”

Mara kept her gaze on him, though her fingers curled beneath the table.

“Ask me again,” she said.

Vale’s expression hardened. “I will.”

The rifle came out of the case like a bad memory.

I laid the pieces on the table and put them together by feel, not because the dark demanded it, but because ritual keeps a man from asking questions too early. Metal met metal. The old room held its breath. I checked what needed checking and left the rest to the hands that had done this too many times.

Across the street, the target’s window glowed yellow.

A man lived behind that light. Maybe he laughed at bad jokes. Maybe he called somebody every night just to hear them say they were home. The file had reduced him to a name, a photograph, and a sum of money. The city had done the rest: rain on the glass, traffic groaning below, every human thing blurred into distance.

People like to say a job is only a job. They say it when the rent is due, when the past is close behind, when a clean shirt costs more than a clean conscience. I’d said it myself. The lie fit in the mouth like a cigarette—easy to hold, hard to quit.

I finished the preparation and sat still.

The room offered its usual counsel: the clock ticking, the radiator knocking, my own pulse making a fool of itself. I thought about walking away. Then I thought about the people who’d be waiting for me if I did. Neither thought made me noble. That was the trouble with morality. It didn’t open doors. It only made you notice which ones you’d already shut.

The yellow window went dark.

For a moment, the city was only rain and glass.

I lowered my hands. The work was ready. I wasn’t sure I was.

Rain threaded down the brick walls and gathered in the cracks of the alley, turning the pavement black. It carried the blood toward the storm drain in thin, diluted ribbons.

Detective Mara Venn stopped at the tape. The uniform on the near post looked pale under the blue wash of the patrol lights.

“Found him at 04:12,” he said. “Delivery driver. No wallet.”

Venn ducked under the tape. Her boots made a soft sucking sound in the muck.

The dead man lay on his side beside a stack of flattened cardboard, one arm bent beneath him. His coat had been opened in several places. The rain had darkened the fabric until it clung to him, and a loose button ticked against the pavement whenever the wind came down the alley. His face was turned toward the wall.

She looked at the scene in order: the body, the ground around it, the fire escape above, the mouth of the alley. Not at the whole of it. The whole was a story, and stories were how people got ahead of the evidence.

A sour, metallic smell rose through the damp: blood, wet wool, old garbage. Beneath it was the city’s ordinary stink, grease from the takeaway vent and the rank sweetness of a blocked drain. The air was cold enough to tighten her fingers inside her gloves.

“Any weapon?” she asked.

“Nothing obvious.”

“Then don’t make it obvious by moving anything.”

The officer shut his mouth.

Venn crouched. Rain tapped the brim of her hat. She noted the shallow drag marks in the grit, the scuffed heel near the curb, a cigarette crushed flat under the victim’s hand. The man’s skin had taken on the waxy gray of the morning. His wedding ring was still there. A clean band of skin showed where his watch had been.

She wrote that down.

Behind her, a camera shutter clicked. The sound seemed too bright for the alley.

“Whoever did this knew the blind spots,” the officer said.

“Maybe.” Venn straightened slowly, letting her knees complain. “Or maybe they were lucky.”

She looked up at the windows above them. Most were dark. One held a square of yellow light, then went black.

“Get the building’s access logs. And the businesses on both ends of the block. Nobody leaves with a story until we know what they actually saw.”

The rain kept working at the scene, softening the edges, carrying what it could. Venn watched the gutter. The water ran clear now.

She turned away before the alley could become a picture in her mind. It was a place, a body, a set of facts. The rest would have to wait.

“I put in what’s necessary.”

“And if I change my mind?”

“Then the deposit remains spent.”

The client looked up. “That’s your answer?”

“It’s the relevant one.”

The client signed. The producer closed the folder and stood.

“Pleasure doing business,” the client said.

The first time Mara tried, she couldn’t make herself look at the food.

They had wrapped it in a strip of silver emergency blanket and set it on a flat stone between them. No one called it by its name. They called it *what was left*, or *the only chance*, or simply *it*. The wind moved over the wreckage with a thin, steady hiss.

Mara’s hands shook so badly that Eli had to steady the cup of melted snow she was holding.

“You don’t have to,” he said.

She looked at him. His lips were cracked. His eyes kept drifting toward the bundle.

“Yes,” she said. “I do.”

But when she reached for it, her body refused. Her fingers stopped an inch above the silver blanket. Her mind filled the gap with ordinary things: the deadbolt on her apartment door, her mother’s laugh, the taste of toast. Then, underneath those memories, came the thought she had been fighting since morning: *If I don’t eat, I will die.*

It was not a brave thought. It was not noble. It was a plain, cold fact.

Mara shut her eyes. She told herself she wasn’t choosing this. The mountain had chosen; the crash had chosen. She was only agreeing to remain alive.

That distinction held for a moment. It was enough.

She lifted the first bite to her mouth. Her throat tightened, and she nearly dropped it. Eli turned away, giving her the small mercy of not being watched.

Mara swallowed.

Nothing changed. The sky stayed white. The wind kept hissing. Her hands still shook.

Then her stomach, which had been a hollow ache for two days, cramped around the food. She pressed a fist to it and bent forward, ashamed of the relief that came with the pain.

Eli asked, quietly, “Can you do another?”

Mara stared at the silver blanket. She thought of the person who had been beside her in the plane, who had shared a scarf and told a terrible joke as the engines failed. She thought of the promise she’d made when they found him: *We’ll get you home.*

“I don’t know,” she said.

And because she didn’t know, she reached again.

The boy never came back.

She looked past him, at the glass bells and the faces inside them. “You’ve made them look peaceful.”

Mara’s eyes stopped on the woman in blue. “Did she ask you to remember her?”

The room seemed to hold its breath.

He told himself that this was how love worked: a thousand careful adjustments, until nothing could change again.

Thud.

The dark settled gently over everything.

The note was folded into a square and tucked beneath the dog’s empty water bowl.

Detective Mara Velez almost missed it. The kitchen had been searched once already; drawers stood open, cupboard doors yawning over the silent room. Outside, rain ticked against the windows. Somewhere upstairs, a clock kept counting.

She pulled on fresh gloves and eased the paper free.

The handwriting was careful, each letter printed separately, as if the writer had taken special care to make it easy to read.

> Dear Detective,  
>   
> I had to hurt Mabel because she kept scratching at the cellar door. She knew Dad was down there. She wanted someone to find him.  
>   
> I told her he was sleeping, but she wouldn’t listen. She kept making noise, and then people would come, and then they would take him away from me.  
>   
> Mabel isn’t bad. She just thinks every closed door should open.  
>   
> I’m sorry she doesn’t understand.  
>   
> Eli

Velez read it twice. The child’s father had been found in the cellar that morning. Eli, eight years old, was at the station with a social worker, drinking hot chocolate from a paper cup. The first officers had described him as quiet. Helpful, even. He had let them in and shown them where to look.

A soft whine came from the hall.

Velez lowered the note. Mabel lay on a blanket beside the radiator, wrapped in a towel. The veterinarian said she would live. Her eyes followed Velez, wary but alert.

The detective looked back at the last line.

*I’m sorry she doesn’t understand.*

Not *I’m sorry I hurt her.* Not *I wish I hadn’t.*

Velez slid the note into an evidence sleeve. In the clear plastic, the careful letters looked even smaller.

Outside, a car door shut. The social worker would be bringing Eli to the station soon.

Mabel gave another faint whine.

Velez crouched beside her. “It’s all right,” she whispered, though she wasn’t sure which of them she meant.

At first, Mara thought it was a rash. A pale seam appeared along her wrist, then widened, the skin peeling back in thin, translucent curls. Beneath it, the new flesh was dark and strangely smooth, as if something underneath had been waiting for air.

Her ribs shifted under her shirt, one by one, pressing outward before sinking into a new arrangement. Each movement brought a burst of pain—and, afterward, a terrible sense of relief. Her body was learning a shape it preferred.

She stopped calling the doctor after she caught her reflection smiling when she wasn’t. Soon, even the mirror seemed unnecessary. She could hear the people in the neighboring apartments: their heartbeats fluttering behind walls, their frightened whispers. The sounds stirred an appetite she couldn’t name.

Mara used to apologize when she bumped into someone. Now she watched them stumble and wondered how easily they might break. The thought should have horrified her. Instead, it felt practical.

On the seventh night, another strip of skin sloughed from her shoulder. She let it fall to the floor and stepped over it.

By morning, the woman in the mirror had Mara’s face only in pieces. And when she tried to remember why that mattered, the thought slid away, smooth and clean as a shed skin.

Mara looked up from her hands. “You always announce it like the weather?”

“I was told to.”

“Then you can tell me something else.”

He stood on the other side of the table, his cap turning slowly between his fingers. “What would you like to hear?”

“What it’s like outside.”

He glanced toward the narrow window, though there was nothing to see through it but darkness. “Cold. There’s rain.”

“Hard rain?”

“Not yet.”

“Good.” She nodded, as if he’d given her useful news. “I always hated hard rain.”

The executioner sat. He kept his hands on the cap.

“Do you think I did it?” she asked.

He did not answer at once.

“That’s not one of the questions I’m supposed to answer,” he said.

“I didn’t ask what you were supposed to do.”

“No.”

“Do you?”

“I don’t know you.”

“You’ve read the file.”

“I’ve read enough files to know paper can make anyone look simple.”

A faint smile crossed her face. “That’s almost an answer.”

“It’s the only honest one I have.”

She looked at him for a while. “My brother used to say that. Then he’d lie.”

“Was he older?”

“By six years. He thought that made him wise.”

“Did it?”

“No. But it made him louder.”

The executioner set down his cap. “Would you like me to pass a message to someone?”

“I’ve written them all down.”

“Anyone you forgot?”

Mara rubbed her thumb over a pale mark on her wrist. “Tell my daughter the lilacs came back.”

He waited.

“She’ll know what that means,” Mara said. “She planted them with me when she was little. We thought they’d died the first winter.”

“I’ll tell her.”

“Don’t say it gently. She hates when people are gentle with her.”

“I’ll try to say it plainly.”

“Thank you.”

A clock ticked somewhere beyond the door.

“How long have you been doing this?” she asked.

“Long enough.”

“That’s not a number.”

“No.”

“Do you sleep?”

“Sometimes.”

“Do you dream?”

He looked at the cap between them. “Sometimes.”

“About the people?”

“About the rooms.”

She considered that. “Rooms are easier.”

“Yes.”

“Not for the people in them.”

“No.”

For a moment, neither spoke. Mara leaned back in her chair.

“Do you have children?”

“One son.”

“Does he know what you do?”

“He knows what I do for work.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No.”

“Will you tell him?”

“I don’t know.”

She nodded. “That’s an honest answer.”

The clock continued. The rain began—not hard, just enough to whisper against the window.

“Five minutes,” the executioner had said. Mara listened to the rain.

“Will you remember me?” she asked.

“I’ll remember your name.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

She stood when the knock came at the door.

“Elias,” she said.

He looked up, surprised that she knew his name.

“Tell my daughter the lilacs came back.”

“I will.”

“And don’t make it gentle.”

“I won’t.”

The door opened. Mara took one breath, then another, and walked toward it.

The first shovelful struck the lid with a hollow **whump**.

Mara jerked awake, sucking in a breath that had nowhere to go. Her shoulders hit wood. Her knees were already drawn tight against her chest; there was no room to stretch, no room even to turn her head. The darkness pressed close on every side, warm and stale with the smell of varnish and earth.

Another **whump**.

Dust sifted through the narrow seams above her face. It touched her lips. She tried to spit it out, but her mouth had gone dry.

“No,” she said, though the word barely made a sound.

The next load landed harder. The lid shuddered above her forehead. Dirt rattled down its length, a rough, heavy applause. She beat both fists against the wood.

“Help!”

The coffin returned the word to her, smaller and flatter. She struck again. Pain bloomed in her knuckles. Above, another shovelful fell.

**Whump.**

Each impact seemed to steal a little space. The coffin had not moved, but the air had changed—thicker now, used, impossible to draw deep enough. She gulped at it anyway. Her chest tightened. Her heartbeat filled the box, frantic and loud.

She pressed her cheek to the lid and listened. For a moment there was only the rasp of dirt sliding over wood.

Then footsteps. Fading.

Mara pulled in a shallow breath. The air tasted of dust and panic. She held it, afraid that even breathing would use too much, until her lungs began to burn.

Above her, the earth settled with a soft, final hiss.

The operating room had once been a school gym. The basketball lines still showed faintly beneath the antiseptic shine, pale arcs circling the tables where the citizens lay strapped down.

Mara heard the machines before she saw them: the patient rhythm of pumps, the dry clicking of instruments, the low hum that filled the room like a second atmosphere. A screen above her displayed her name, then replaced it with a number.

“Asset 8-441,” said the surgeon.

She tried to turn her head. The restraints held her gently, which somehow made them worse. A mask pressed over her mouth, smelling of plastic and wintergreen. Someone told her to be still. Someone else said the conversion would be efficient.

Then the pain began—not as a sharp point, but as a bright, spreading certainty. Her body became a place where strangers were working. She could feel herself being divided into tasks: a hand for lifting, a back for carrying, lungs calibrated to keep pace with the factory shift. Each new sensation arrived with a command tone and a number attached.

“Response delay acceptable.”

“Grip strength within range.”

Mara tried to say her brother’s name. The word caught behind the mask. She tried again, but the sound that came out was a thin electronic chirp. A technician glanced at the monitor and made a note.

Around her, other tables trembled. A man sobbed until the rhythm of his breathing changed; the machine beside him adjusted, patient and precise. No one looked up. The staff had learned not to meet the eyes of people who were still themselves.

When the straps were finally released, Mara sat upright without meaning to. Her new joints moved smoothly, obediently, as if her body had already forgotten the old way. A door opened. Beyond it, workers waited in a line beneath a sign that read **PRODUCTIVITY IS FREEDOM**.

She remembered the gym’s old scoreboard, the one that used to flash the winning team’s name. Now it showed her number.

For a moment, she reached for the memory of her brother—his laugh, the gap between his front teeth, the way he used to call her Mare.

The memory flickered.

A prompt appeared in her vision: **REPORT TO STATION 12.**

Her feet carried her forward.

The first scene was beautiful.

Mara Vale hated herself for noticing.

It was a narrow room above a shuttered florist’s shop, its windows washed blue by the dawn. The victim lay beside the counter, one hand open, the other curled against his chest. Around him, paper-wrapped stems had spilled from their buckets. White lilies, yellow ranunculus, a scattering of green leaves. The emergency lights turned everything pale and still.

Mara stood at the threshold while the photographer worked.

“Don’t move anything,” she said, though no one had.

The room seemed arranged for a painting: the diagonal of the counter, the long sweep of flowers, the dark line of the man’s coat. Even the rain on the window appeared deliberate, each drop catching the blue light. Mara had spent twenty years teaching herself to see only what mattered. She made a list in her notebook. Door. Window. Counter. Body. Flowers.

Then she crossed out *flowers* and wrote *scattered merchandise*.

That was how she kept herself honest.

In the weeks that followed, the photographs returned to her in fragments. Not the face of the dead man—she refused that, at first—but the cold light, the paper sleeves, the open hand. She studied the images after work, telling herself she was searching for an overlooked fact. She enlarged corners and shadows. She watched the scene appear and disappear beneath the cursor.

At home, she began arranging ordinary things without meaning to: a cup beside the sink, a book left open on the table. When she noticed, she moved them back.

The dead man’s name was Julian Rook. He had been sixty-one, a florist, a brother, a patient listener, according to the people who knew him. His sister brought a photograph to the station: Julian at twenty, laughing in a greenhouse, dirt on his cheek. Mara pinned it above her desk.

The second scene was in an old concert hall, where a woman had been found beneath the balcony. Empty rows rose behind her, dark as a gathering crowd. A shaft of late sun reached across the floor and stopped just short of her shoes.

Mara felt the familiar, shameful click in her mind—the sense of a composition settling into place.

Then she saw the woman’s handbag, tipped open beside her. A packet of tissues. A bus pass. A child’s drawing, folded twice and softened at the creases. In the picture, a blue house leaned beneath a huge orange sun.

The scene changed. It was no longer a study in shadow and light. It was a place where someone had been interrupted on the way home.

That evening, Mara took the photograph of Julian down from the wall and held it for a long time. His sister had written on the back: *He always kept the first flower from every new shipment for our mother.*

Mara returned to the florist’s shop the next morning. The investigators had cleared it, but the air still smelled faintly of wet leaves. She stood where she had stood before and tried to see the room without its angles.

She saw Julian’s open hand.

She saw the work he had been doing.

She saw a life that the crime had not made beautiful, and that beauty could not repair.

After that, Mara still noticed the light. She noticed the lines, the careful silences of a room after violence. She was a forensic investigator; noticing was her work. But she stopped calling the scenes beautiful.

In her reports, she wrote what had happened.

And, whenever she could, she wrote who had been there.

The alley held the day’s rain in its cracks, and the city’s noise thinned to a distant murmur.

Mara pressed one hand to the brick wall. The other clutched the stranger’s coat, though she could no longer remember deciding to hold on. Beneath his stillness, she felt a tremor—something barely contained.

“Please,” she whispered.

His eyes lifted to hers. In the darkness they caught the thin light from a streetlamp, pale and bright as coins.

The hunger had been gnawing at him for hours. Now it filled the alley, close and hot as breath. He leaned in, and his hand settled against her shoulder—not cruelly, but with a certainty that made her struggle feel useless.

His fangs pierced the skin at her throat. A sharp sting; then a spreading warmth. Mara stiffened, fingers tightening in his coat. The vampire shut his eyes as if the first mouthful had silenced some unbearable pain.

The bricks shifted beneath her palm. She tried to push him away, but her arm moved sluggishly, as though the night had turned it to water. Her heartbeat thudded hard, then softer, each beat farther apart. The stranger held her upright while the alley tilted around them.

At last he drew back.

Mara slid down the wall, breathing shallowly. Two small wounds darkened her collar. She was awake, but the strength had gone from her limbs, leaving her cold and trembling.

For a moment, the vampire watched her with something like regret.

Then the hunger stirred again, and his face vanished into the dark.

The pistol lay between them on the table.

Mara stared at it as if it might speak first.

Across the room, Eli and Tomas knelt with their hands tied. They had been friends since they were children—before the war, before the city burned, before every promise became something you made with your fingers crossed. Now a man in a gray coat stood behind them, watch in hand.

“Choose,” he said. “One dies. The other walks out.”

Mara’s mouth had gone dry. She tried to look at Eli, but his face was bruised and swollen; one eye had nearly closed. Tomas was watching her steadily, as though he could lend her enough courage to make this simple.

Neither begged. That was worse.

“Take me,” Eli said.

Tomas gave a faint, humorless laugh. “You always were bad at volunteering other people.”

The man in gray checked his watch.

Mara felt the seconds as pressure behind her eyes. She tried to find a reason—some fair measure, some rule that would turn this into anything but betrayal. Eli had saved her on the bridge. Tomas had stayed behind when her brother was sick. Each memory rose like evidence, and every piece condemned her.

“Please,” she whispered. She did not know to whom.

Eli shifted on his knees. “Mara. Look at me.”

She did.

He had a scar at his hairline from the day they’d fallen out of an apple tree. She remembered him laughing while blood ran down his temple, insisting it was only a scratch. The memory struck so sharply that, for a moment, she was back in the sun.

“Choose Tomas,” Eli said.

Tomas shut his eyes. “Don’t.”

“I’m not asking you.” Eli’s voice broke. “I’m asking her.”

Mara’s hand moved before she could stop it. Her finger extended toward Tomas.

The man in gray nodded once.

Tomas opened his eyes. He looked at Mara, and she saw the instant he understood—not the choice, but the terror behind it. He tried to smile. The effort failed.

“It’s all right,” he said.

It wasn’t. They both knew it.

The man in gray raised the pistol.

Mara turned away at the last second. The shot cracked through the room. Something struck the wall behind her with a wet, splintering sound. Tomas fell sideways, his shoulder hitting the floor first. Red spread across his shirt, dark at the center, bright along the torn edge.

Mara made a noise she did not recognize as her own.

Eli surged against his bonds. The guards dragged him upright. He was alive, breathing hard, staring at Tomas—and then at her.

The man in gray set the pistol back on the table.

“You chose,” he said.

Mara looked at the blood working its way between the floorboards. She had imagined that choice would end when the gun fired. Instead it had opened into a vast, silent place, and she was standing in it alone.

The first thing Daniel noticed was the smell.

It came through the crack beneath the basement door: damp earth, old pennies, and something sweet gone rotten. He stood at the top of the stairs with a flashlight in one hand and his phone in the other, listening to the rain rattle against the house.

“Martin?” he called.

No answer.

His neighbor’s back door had been hanging open when Daniel came over to return a borrowed ladder. Martin was fastidious about everything—his clipped hedges, his spotless kitchen, the little brass number on his mailbox. An open door was so unlike him that Daniel had stepped inside to check.

Now the basement door was ajar, and a thin line of yellow light showed beneath it.

Daniel should have left. He knew that. Instead, he pushed the door.

The stairs groaned under his weight. The smell thickened as he descended, clinging to the back of his throat. At the bottom, the flashlight beam found shelves of paint cans, a workbench, a folded tarp. Then it swept over a row of glass-fronted cabinets.

Inside them were objects arranged with the care of a museum display.

Watches. Rings. A child’s red mitten. A pair of cracked glasses. Each sat on a small white card, labeled in Martin’s neat handwriting with a date and a name.

Daniel stopped breathing.

The next cabinet held photographs—dozens of them—of strangers caught in ordinary moments. A woman waiting for a bus. A man carrying groceries. A teenager with headphones, laughing at something beyond the frame. Beneath each photograph was another name and date.

On the workbench lay a row of keys, all tagged. Beside them, a stained kitchen knife rested on a folded towel. The blade had been cleaned, but not well enough. A dark smear remained near the handle.

Daniel backed away, bumping the shelves. A glass jar toppled and shattered.

The sound rang through the basement.

From somewhere upstairs came the click of the back door closing.

Daniel’s phone felt slick in his hand. He tried to unlock it and missed the button. His flashlight trembled across the wall, revealing one last display: a single empty hook, with a white card beneath it.

The card read: **DANIEL PRICE.**

At the top of the stairs, someone began to descend.

“Found my collection,” Martin said.

Daniel turned toward the narrow window set high in the far wall. It was too small to climb through. The stairs were blocked by Martin’s shadow.

Then Daniel saw the old coal chute, half-hidden behind the workbench. He lunged for it, knocking a box of tools to the floor. Metal clattered. Martin’s steps quickened.

Daniel shoved at the chute’s warped wooden panel. It gave way with a shriek. Cold rain blew in through the opening.

Behind him, Martin reached the bottom stair.

Daniel squeezed through, scraping his shoulder, and dropped into the alley behind the houses. He ran barefoot through the rain to the street, screaming for help.

By the time the police arrived, Martin was gone.

They found the basement exactly as Daniel had described it: the cabinets, the photographs, the labeled objects, the empty hook.

And on the kitchen table upstairs, beside Martin’s untouched cup of tea, they found a fresh white card.

It bore Daniel’s name.

The date was tomorrow’s.

“Long day?” someone asked.

“Must be,” he said, though his voice had gone thin.

He reached for his glass and missed it by an inch. The sound of the stem tapping the table was small, but it seemed to silence the room. He tried to smile. Color had drained from his face, leaving a grayness beneath the candlelight.

The conversation stumbled on around him. Someone asked whether he wanted air. He nodded, then shook his head, as if the question had arrived from a great distance. His palm flattened against the tablecloth. His breathing came shallow and uneven.

For one instant, he looked straight at me.

There was no accusation in his eyes. Only confusion—and, worse, trust.

I lowered my gaze to my untouched wine. The bishop’s story had reached its punch line, but nobody laughed.

The captain had the plank lowered over the side at sunset.

It was a narrow thing, slick with spray, stretching from the rail into a sea gone black beneath the ship. Below, fins cut slow circles through the water.

“Last chance,” Captain Vane said.

The mutineer, Elias, stared down. His wrists were bound behind him. He tried to answer, but the wind stole the words. Around him, the crew stood silent, their faces pale in the dying light.

Vane leaned close. “You wanted command. Take a step toward it.”

Elias’s boots touched the plank. The ship creaked. Behind him, someone muttered a prayer.

He walked.

At first he kept his eyes on the far end, where the sea met the sky. Then the plank dipped under his weight, and he looked down. A fin swept past, close enough to stir the water. His breath broke into a sob.

“Captain—”

“Keep walking.”

Elias took another step. The plank shuddered. A wave slapped its underside, and he stumbled, catching himself with a bound hand against the rail. The crew flinched as one.

Vane gave a small nod.

A sailor struck the plank’s support loose. It dropped, and Elias vanished into the sea.

The water erupted. Fins converged, churning the dark surface into foam. Elias’s shout rose once above the crash of waves, then was swallowed by the noise. Red spread briefly across the water before the tide pulled it apart.

No one cheered. Even Vane watched in silence as the circling fins drifted away.

Then he turned to the crew.

“Anyone else wishing to test the captain’s mercy?”

By the seventh night, Elias had stopped sleeping.

He sat at the kitchen table with every light burning, listening to the house settle around him. The old pipes knocked in the walls. The refrigerator hummed. Rain worried at the windows.

Then came the dripping.

Elias stared at the ceiling. One drop. Another. Slow and patient.

He stood, chair scraping behind him, and followed the sound down the hall. It led to the basement door.

“No,” he whispered.

The dripping continued.

He had scrubbed the cellar floor until his hands split. He had painted over the stain, then painted over it again. There was nothing left to clean. Nothing left to find.

At the foot of the stairs, a woman stood in her yellow raincoat.

Mara’s hair hung in wet ropes across her face. One sleeve was torn. She held her head at an awkward angle, the way it had rested against the stones when he left her there.

Elias seized the banister. “You’re dead.”

Her face lifted. Beneath the strands of hair, one eye was open.

“You said you’d come back for me,” she said.

He shut his eyes. The voice remained—not in the room, but inside his skull, intimate as a thought. When he opened them, the cellar was empty.

For a little while, he could pretend.

Then the house began to fill with water.

It ran beneath the doors in black threads. It climbed the stairs without a sound, carrying the smell of river mud and cold iron. Elias backed into the kitchen, slipped, and caught himself against the table. His hands came away wet.

Across the room, Mara sat in his chair.

“You were afraid,” she said.

“I didn’t mean—”

“You looked at me.”

He pressed both hands over his ears. The lights flickered. In each brief darkness, she was closer: beside the stove, at the doorway, right in front of him. Her pale fingers touched his cheek.

He struck at her. His fist met empty air and sent him crashing against the cupboard.

When the lights steadied, he was alone. A glass lay shattered on the floor. In the dark window above the sink, his reflection stared back at him—and behind it stood Mara, dripping quietly onto the kitchen tiles.

Elias spun around.

Nothing.

He began to laugh. It came out in little broken bursts, and soon he couldn’t tell whether he was laughing or sobbing. He fell to his knees and whispered her name, again and again, as if repetition could become a door he might walk through.

At dawn, the rain stopped.

The house was dry. The window showed only his own face: gray, hollow, and wild-eyed.

Then, from somewhere beneath the floorboards, came three soft knocks.

Elias stopped breathing.

A pause.

Then Mara’s voice, calm as a promise:

“Come get me.”

The siren sounded once, low and mournful, from the towers beyond the trees.

Mara stumbled through the rain, one hand pressed to her ribs. Behind her, the searchlights combed the forest in slow white sweeps. The city called it the Pursuit: one night a month when the wealthy could buy a numbered coat, take a rifle into the quarantine belt, and hunt whoever had been sentenced to run.

Her number—417—was stitched across her back in red.

She reached the old culvert and dropped to her knees. The tunnel was too narrow to crawl through with her injured leg. She heard boots in the wet leaves behind her, unhurried.

“End of the course,” called a man’s voice.

Mara turned. A hunter stood between the trees, his polished mask reflecting the searchlight. He carried a rifle, but he kept it pointed at the ground. That was part of the broadcast rules: the capture had to be clean.

“I’m not going back,” she said.

“None of you are.” He lowered the rifle and held up a small black device. “Hands where I can see them.”

She looked past him, toward the dark beyond the searchlights. For a moment, she considered making him shoot. Then the beam found her face, and the forest filled with the distant crackle of commentators celebrating.

Mara raised her hands.

The hunter pressed the device to the number on her coat. It chirped. Somewhere above them, a scoreboard flashed from **RUNNING** to **CLAIMED**.

He unclipped a silver badge from his lapel and fastened it to his own chest.

“Prize secured,” he said.

Behind the mask, his voice sounded almost embarrassed.

The drones descended, their red lenses blinking. The broadcast began with applause. Mara watched the badge catch the light and understood: he hadn’t come for her money, or her name, or even the points.

He had come to be seen winning.

The shelling stopped so suddenly that Thomas heard the rain.

It ticked against the trench boards and ran in thin streams down the walls. Somewhere behind him a man was coughing. Somewhere ahead, in the torn strip of earth between the lines, someone was calling for his mother.

Thomas gripped his shovel with both hands. Its wooden handle was slick with mud. He had been using it to clear a fallen brace when the enemy soldier came over the lip of the trench.

For half a second they simply stared at each other.

The man was young, though Thomas had thought all the enemy were older. His cap was gone. There was a white bandage around his forehead, darkening at one edge. He held a rifle with no bayonet, and his face had the fixed, bewildered look of someone who had taken a wrong turn in a familiar house.

Then the man lunged.

Thomas swung.

The shovel struck with a dull, ugly sound—not the sharp crack he’d imagined, but something heavier, intimate. The soldier staggered against the trench wall. Thomas smelled wet wool, mud, and the copper stink of blood. The man grabbed at him, fingers closing on his tunic, and they went down together in the sludge.

Thomas’s cheek hit the ground. He could feel the other man’s breath against his ear, quick and hot. The shovel was trapped beneath them. They fought without skill, without room, their boots scraping for purchase on the slick boards. Thomas saw the bandage slipping. He saw one frightened eye, close enough to reflect the grey sky.

The soldier reached for Thomas’s throat.

Thomas pulled the shovel free and brought it down again.

The struggle stopped.

For a moment, Thomas stayed where he was, kneeling over the body, both hands locked around the handle. His arms trembled as if the blow were still passing through them. The other man’s eyes remained open. Rain gathered on his lashes.

“Tom?” someone shouted behind him.

Thomas looked over his shoulder but couldn’t answer. His mouth had filled with the taste of iron, though he couldn’t tell whether he’d bitten his tongue. He crawled backward until his spine struck the trench wall. The shovel slipped from his fingers and landed in the mud.

He stared at his hands. They were shaking. He rubbed them on his coat, then rubbed them again, harder, as if the feeling on them were dirt that could be scraped away.

A medic pushed past, muttering. Someone else dragged the body by the collar. Thomas watched the young man’s boots trail through the mud, heels knocking softly against the boards.

The coughing behind him began again.

Thomas pressed his palms over his ears, but the trench was full of sounds: rain, boots, distant guns, the thin call from the ground beyond the parapet. Underneath them all was the dull sound of the shovel striking.

He had expected terror to make him feel less human. Instead it had left him painfully, absurdly aware of everything: the cold seeping through his knees, the mud drying at the corner of his mouth, the trembling in his fingers. And the fact that, somewhere, someone might be waiting for the man he had killed to come home.

When the sergeant told him to get back to work, Thomas picked up the shovel.

He held it by the very end of the handle, careful not to look at the blade.

In the Republic, the law made no distinction between a hungry hand and a dangerous one. Stealing a loaf, skipping a tax, speaking against the Council—each could earn a place on the public platform. The executions were called **Civic Lessons**. Attendance was compulsory for schools and government offices, and vendors sold hot tea along the square.

The boy on the platform looked younger than the notices had said. His name was Tomas Vale; he was sixteen, and the loaf he had taken was still listed in the charge as evidence. His coat hung loose at the sleeves. He kept glancing over the crowd, searching faces, though no one knew whether he was looking for someone or simply trying to find a way out.

At first, the square gave the officials what they wanted: silence.

Then someone laughed too loudly at a joke near the fountain. The sound snagged in the air and died. A woman pulled her daughter close and turned the girl’s face against her shoulder. Two clerks in gray uniforms stared rigidly ahead, lips moving with the pledge they were required to recite. An old man took off his cap.

The prosecutor read the sentence. Tomas flinched at the word *bread*. Not at the charge, not at the law—at the bread.

A murmur moved through the crowd. It wasn’t a chant, not yet. It was the sound of people remembering empty cupboards, ration lines, the price of flour. A baker in the front row lowered his eyes. Somewhere behind him, a child whispered, “He was hungry.”

The guards stepped forward. The crowd shifted as one body, but nobody moved to stop them. That was the lesson the Republic meant to teach: not that the law was just, but that fear could make witnesses out of everyone.

When the bell rang, several people looked away. A few kept watching, as if refusing to look might be counted against them too. And from the back of the square came the soft, unmistakable sound of someone crying.
